summary: Judges 19 (30 verses) continues the story of cycle of sin. Starting with 'In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a certain Levite living on the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim, who took for himself a co', it moves through themes of cycle of sin, judge-deliverer and calls readers toward need for king.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows cycle of sin lived out in canaan, cycles of oppression. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a certain Levite living on the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim, who took for himself a concubine out of Bethlehem Judah.
Behold, an old man came from his work out of the field at evening. Now the man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he lived in Gibeah; but the men of the place were Benjamites.

It was so, that all who saw it said, “Such a deed has not been done or seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt to this day! Consider it, take counsel, and speak.

questions.question: What is happening in Judges 19?
questions.answer: In 30 verses, this chapter judges 19 (30 verses) continues the story of cycle of sin. starting with 'in those days, when there was no king in israel, there was a certain levite living on the farther side of the hill country of ephraim, who took for himself a co', it moves through themes of cycle of sin, judge-deliverer and calls readers toward need for king. The setting is canaan, cycles of oppression, written to israel in monarchy. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Judges and why 19 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally anonymous, prophetic history, addressed to israel in monarchy around ~1050 bc events, compiled later. This chapter fits the book's purpose as cycle narrative — its themes of cycle of sin, judge-deliverer build on what came before.

questions.question: Are there any difficult words here?
questions.answer: Scan for names, places, or repeated abstract words like righteousness, covenant, or glory. The glossary below defines up to 3 that show up most. Ask: who is this person, what does this word mean in everyday terms?

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through cycle of sin and judge-deliverer, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 9 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'When the man rose up to depart, he, and his concubine, and his servant, his father-in-law, the young lady’s father, said to him, “Behold, now the day draws toward evening, please s...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about cycle of sin. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
